plan.contextChunk: This figure is a coordinate plane carrying four straight lines, each in a different color with arrowheads on both ends and tagged with a Roman numeral. The horizontal axis is labeled x and numbered from -7 to 7, the vertical axis is labeled y and numbered from -5 to 5, and a light gray unit grid fills the plotting region. Line I is orange and by far the steepest, rising from below the x-axis at the lower left and exiting through the top of the grid just right of the y-axis, where its label sits. Line II is light blue and the shallowest, entering at the left near x equal to -6.5 on the x-axis, crossing the y-axis at 3, and climbing to about x equal to 4, y equal to 5. Line III is teal, crossing the y-axis at -3 and the x-axis near x equal to 1.5 before rising to that same upper right region. Line IV is dark blue and the only line with a negative slope, entering at the upper left, crossing the y-axis at 3, and descending to roughly x equal to 4, y equal to -4.5. Color and numeral identify the lines, leaving steepness and direction as the properties to read off. The plot supports an exercise in pairing four given linear equations with the correct lines.

interactionPlan.concept: In y = mx + b, the slope m controls a line's steepness and direction while the intercept b sets where it crosses the y-axis, so any line on a graph can be matched to its equation by reading those two numbers off the picture.
elements: Cartesian grid with light gray unit gridlines spanning x from -7 to 7 and y from -5 to 5
Horizontal x-axis with arrowheads both ends, labeled 'x', ticks and numerals -7 through 7
Vertical y-axis with arrowheads both ends, labeled 'y', ticks and numerals -5 through 5
Line I: orange, very steep positive slope (about m = 3, b = 0.5), arrowheads both ends, label 'I' near its top exit just right of the y-axis
Line II: light blue, shallow positive slope (about m = 0.5, b = 3), arrowheads both ends, label 'II' at upper right near x = 4
Line III: teal, moderate positive slope (about m = 2, b = -3), arrowheads both ends, label 'III' at upper right, crosses x-axis near x = 1.5
Line IV: dark blue, negative slope (about m = -2, b = 3), arrowheads both ends, label 'IV' at lower right near x = 4
Candidate line: dashed magenta/purple movable line y = mx + b controlled by the sliders, arrowheads both ends
y-intercept marker dot on the candidate line at (0, b) with coordinate callout
Rise-over-run staircase markers (horizontal run segment and vertical rise segment with labeled lengths) drawn on the selected line when clicked
Readout box showing the candidate line's equation y = mx + b with current values
Legend / color key pairing each Roman numeral with its color

interactions.teaches: That the sign of m decides whether the line rises or falls and the magnitude of m decides how steep it is, while the pivot point at (0, b) never moves.
interactions.label: Slope m of candidate line

interactions.teaches: That b slides the whole line vertically without changing its direction, so two lines with the same steepness are told apart only by where they cut the y-axis.
interactions.label: y-intercept b of candidate line

interactions.teaches: That the visual steepness of a given line is literally rise over run, converting the picture into a numeric slope that can be matched to an equation.
That hiding the reference lines forces the learner to predict m and b from the equation, and showing them confirms or refutes the match.
interactions.label: Reference lines

demo_steps.title: Four lines, four equations
demo_steps.narration: Four lines cross the same grid: orange I is steepest, light blue II is the shallowest, teal III rises from -3, and dark blue IV is the only one falling. Your job is to read each line's slope and intercept.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the candidate line
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slope slider and watch the dashed line pivot about the origin. Large positive m gives a steep climb like line I; small positive m gives a shallow climb like line II.

demo_steps.title: Negative slope flips the direction
demo_steps.narration: Push m below zero and the dashed line tips the other way — only line IV has this downhill behavior, so its equation must have a negative slope.

demo_steps.title: Lift the line with b
demo_steps.narration: Now raise b to 3. The line keeps its downhill tilt but slides up until it crosses the y-axis at 3 — it lands exactly on line IV. Slope plus intercept pins a line uniquely.

demo_steps.title: Same intercept, different slope
demo_steps.narration: Keep b = 3 and set m = 0.5. The line still passes through (0, 3) but now leans gently upward onto line II — proof that b alone cannot identify a line.

demo_steps.title: Match line III
demo_steps.narration: Click line III to see its rise-over-run staircase, then set m = 2 and b = -3. The dashed candidate overlays it, confirming y = 2x - 3.

demo_steps.title: Test yourself
demo_steps.narration: Hide lines I–IV and try to reproduce line I from memory: a steep positive slope with a small positive intercept. Show them again to check.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A line is completely determined by two readable numbers — how fast it climbs (m) and where it cuts the y-axis (b) — so matching graphs to equations is just reading steepness and crossing point off the picture.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Square-ish coordinate plane with a pale gray unit grid, black axes with double arrowheads, x labeled -7..7 and y labeled -5..5, axis letters 'x' at right and 'y' at top. Four full-width straight lines in the source palette: orange (steepest, ~y = 3x + 0.5, label I near the top just right of the y-axis), light blue (~y = 0.5x + 3, label II at upper right), teal (~y = 2x - 3, label III at upper right, x-intercept near 1.5), dark blue (~y = -2x + 3, label IV at lower right). Each line carries arrowheads at both ends and its Roman numeral in matching color at the end where it exits the grid. Overlay a dashed magenta candidate line driven by the sliders, with a filled dot at (0, b) and an equation readout 'y = mx + b' in the corner. Clicking a line thickens it, dims the others, and draws a right-triangle staircase (horizontal run in gray, vertical rise in the line's color) with the run and rise values labeled plus the resulting slope fraction. Keep the grid subordinate visually so the four colored lines and the dashed candidate read clearly.

discrepancies: Default (step-0) view adds a magenta dashed candidate line 'y = x' running corner-to-corner, plus a magenta dot and '(0, 0)' callout at the origin — none of these exist in the source, so the initial render is not a clean drop-in replacement for the static figure.

The candidate-equation label 'y = x' is drawn on top of the teal 'III' label near (4, 5), producing a hard collision that makes both strings hard to read; the 'II' label also sits right next to the dashed line's arrowhead.

Line I's parameters (m = 3, b = 0.5) put its y-intercept lower than in the source, where the orange line appears to cross the y-axis near y ≈ 1 (x-intercept clearly left of −0.3); the generated orange line crosses x at about −0.17.
The bold axis label 'x' at the right end renders very small/faint next to the arrowhead compared with the prominent bold 'x' and 'y' in the source.

Line labels I–IV are offset along the line direction rather than sitting compactly beside the arrow tips as in the source (e.g. 'IV' sits well below the arrow, 'I' well above), slightly shifting the composition.
evaluation.notes: Grid, axes, four correctly-colored double-arrow lines and the I–IV labels closely reproduce the source and the slider/step/click interactions are genuinely pedagogical, but the always-on magenta dashed candidate line with its '(0,0)' callout clutters the default view and its equation label collides with the 'III' label.
action_items: Hide the dashed candidate line, its origin dot and '(0, 0)' callout in the initial/step-0 state (show them only after the user moves a slider or advances a step) so the default render matches the static source.

Reposition the candidate equation label with simple collision avoidance against the I–IV line labels — e.g. place it mid-line with a perpendicular offset or in a fixed corner box instead of at the arrow tip.
Re-fit line I to the source: use a y-intercept near 1 (e.g. m = 3, b = 1) so its x-intercept lands visibly left of the y-axis as in the original, and update the step-7 narration/target accordingly.
Increase the size/weight of the bold 'x' and 'y' axis labels and nudge them clear of the arrowheads so they read as clearly as in the source.

feedback.rationale: The interaction concept and decomposition are sound; the issues are concrete implementation fixes — hiding the candidate line at step 0, resolving label collisions, adjusting line I's intercept, and enlarging axis labels.

discrepancies: Label placement for II and III is effectively swapped relative to the source: in the original, 'II' sits at the light-blue line's arrow tip (upper area, left of III) and 'III' sits to its lower-right on the teal line; in the render 'III' appears above-left and 'II' below-right, and 'II' is set slightly detached from its arrow tip.

The grid rectangle is clipped at ±6.8 / ±5.3 instead of the source's full ±7 / ±5 cell boundaries, so the outermost tick numerals (−7, 7, ±5) sit essentially on the border rather than outside a clean grid edge as in the original.
Axis letters in the source are italic serif math-style 'x' and 'y'; the render uses bold upright sans-serif, a small stylistic drift (minor).

Reference-lines checkbox is labelled 'Show reference lines I–IV' but is wired through an input id named showCandidate; toggling it off removes the entire source figure content — a confusing default-state control for a drop-in replacement (no visual error at step 0, but the naming is misleading).
evaluation.notes: Very faithful reproduction of the four-line coordinate-grid figure with correct slopes/intercepts, colors, double-headed arrows and tick numerals, plus a rich and pedagogically apt interaction set (slope/intercept sliders, dashed candidate line, click-for-rise/run staircase, 7-step guided tour); only minor label-placement drift (II/III swapped positions) and slightly cropped grid extent keep it from a perfect match.
action_items: Place the 'II' label flush at the light-blue arrow tip and 'III' to its lower-right on the teal arrow, matching the source's relative ordering and offsets.
Extend the grid rectangle to exactly ±7 in x and ±5 in y so the outermost tick numerals sit outside the grid border as in the original.
Rename/retarget the 'Show reference lines I–IV' checkbox id (showCandidate → showReference) and consider disabling it at step 0 so the default state cannot be emptied accidentally.
Use an italic serif style for the bold 'x' and 'y' axis letters to match the textbook typography.

demo_steps.narration: Drag the slope slider and watch the dashed line pivot about the origin. Large positive m gives a steep climb like line I; small positive m gives a shallow climb like line II.

demo_steps.title: Negative slope flips the direction
demo_steps.narration: Push m below zero and the dashed line tips the other way — only line IV has this downhill behavior, so its equation must have a negative slope.

demo_steps.title: Lift the line with b
demo_steps.narration: Now raise b to 3. The line keeps its downhill tilt but slides up until it crosses the y-axis at 3 — it lands exactly on line IV. Slope plus intercept pins a line uniquely.

demo_steps.title: Same intercept, different slope
demo_steps.narration: Keep b = 3 and set m = 0.5. The line still passes through (0, 3) but now leans gently upward onto line II — proof that b alone cannot identify a line.

demo_steps.title: Match line III
demo_steps.narration: Click line III to see its rise-over-run staircase, then set m = 2 and b = -3. The dashed candidate overlays it, confirming y = 2x - 3.

demo_steps.title: Test yourself
demo_steps.narration: Hide lines I–IV and try to reproduce line I from memory: a steep positive slope with a small positive intercept. Show them again to check.

plan.keyInsight: A line is completely determined by two readable numbers — how fast it climbs (m) and where it cuts the y-axis (b) — so matching graphs to equations is just reading steepness and crossing point off the picture.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Square-ish coordinate plane with a pale gray unit grid, black axes with double arrowheads, x labeled -7..7 and y labeled -5..5, axis letters 'x' at right and 'y' at top. Four full-width straight lines in the source palette: orange (steepest, ~y = 3x + 0.5, label I near the top just right of the y-axis), light blue (~y = 0.5x + 3, label II at upper right), teal (~y = 2x - 3, label III at upper right, x-intercept near 1.5), dark blue (~y = -2x + 3, label IV at lower right). Each line carries arrowheads at both ends and its Roman numeral in matching color at the end where it exits the grid. Overlay a dashed magenta candidate line driven by the sliders, with a filled dot at (0, b) and an equation readout 'y = mx + b' in the corner. Clicking a line thickens it, dims the others, and draws a right-triangle staircase (horizontal run in gray, vertical rise in the line's color) with the run and rise values labeled plus the resulting slope fraction. Keep the grid subordinate visually so the four colored lines and the dashed candidate read clearly.

discrepancies: The white text halos behind the y-axis numerals erase chunks of the vertical axis, so the y-axis reads as a broken/dashed line instead of the solid arrowed axis in the source.
The origin label '0' that appears just left/below the origin in the source is omitted in the generated figure.
Line strokes are noticeably thinner than the bold coloured strokes of the source, making the four lines read lighter at inline size (arrowheads are correctly present on both ends, though).

Minor placement drift of the roman-numeral labels: in the source 'I' sits clearly right of the orange arrow tip and 'III' sits below-right of the teal tip; in the render they hug the tips more tightly and 'II'/'III' sit closer together than in the source.
evaluation.notes: Step-0 view is a close, correctly-coloured reproduction of the four-line grid with accurate slopes/intercepts (3/1, 0.5/3, 2/−3, −2/3) and a rich, genuinely pedagogical set of interactions (m/b sliders, reference toggle, rise/run selection, 7-step narrated demo); main blemishes are the halo-broken y-axis, missing origin '0', and slightly thin line weights.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; the remaining issues are purely rendering details (halo-broken y-axis, missing origin '0', thin strokes, label placement) that belong to the generator.
